docs.title: What a JEPA world model actually buys you on a $300 arm
docs.text:
Thesis. On a low-cost, position-controlled arm, a latent world model earns its place as a verifier, not a planner: it reads outcomes and flags surprise, but ranking actions by imagined latents loses to a baseline that just looks at the commanded joints. The gains worth chasing on GPU-poor hardware are in evaluation, data selection and inference engineering, not in bigger policies.

Everything below was run on one SO-101 (6-DoF, STS3215 servos), a wrist and a top camera, a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB, a Mac, and rented GPUs. Total recorded cloud spend across the whole programme: about $27. Every result has a pre-registered pass rule, a report and, where it ran on the arm, the videos.

docs.title: 1. The world model is a verifier, not a planner
docs.text:
Question. Can a small JEPA world model (LeWM, 192-d latent, multi-view, trained on 182 episodes for $3.30) pick better action chunks or detect failures before they happen?

Role tested Gate Result Verdict Rerank 8 VLA-JEPA samples (best-of-N) H0 Samples are bundled (1.08° spread); reranking adds 1.84× latency and a plain mean of the 8 chunks gets 45 % of the oracle gain with no model at all no-go Rank the expert chunk first among 8 (plannable range) G1b best top-1 0.60 (bar 0.80). An action-only baseline, no images, no model, reaches 0.68–0.90 with regret ≈ 0 fail Latent distance as progress / stall signal G6a, G6b Spearman −0.32 to −0.73 (bar −0.8); 32–52 % false stalls fail Read the outcome at the judge's timestamp G10 step 1 AUROC 1.000 (W1), 0.976 (W2) pass Anticipate the outcome 30 steps early (imagined latent) G10 step 2 beats policy identity by +0.18; surprise spikes 1.82× on missed grasps, 2.58× on stalls pass Live surprise check on the Orin NX G11-A 12.8 ms per dual-camera check inside a 33 ms tick pass Live reflex thresholds on fresh rollouts W1-A, G11-B-cal the reflex fires on 42/42 successes; refit catches 3/25 failures at 1/44 false alarms fail → shadow mode Event-anchored grasp check from the imagined latent W1-C1 imagined 0.70 vs current latent 0.82: imagination is 0.12 worse fail

Reading. The model predicts well (G0: K=30 error 0.31 vs copy-last 0.89, reacts to action timing) and reads outcomes perfectly once they have happened. It does not anticipate them reliably enough to act on, and it never beats the commanded joints at ranking. On a position-controlled arm the actions already say where the arm will be; a world model only has something to add on object state and contact, which 182 episodes without counterfactual failures do not teach. This matches D-JEPA's point that prediction accuracy does not make latent distance decision-aligned, and The Planning Limits of Latent World Models on horizon. The world model stays in the stack as a logged signal while failure data accumulates.

docs.text:
Question. What can score a rollout as success or failure on this arm, at what cost?

Judge Data Result Verdict Deterministic top-camera judge (HSV masks + geometry, no learning), at rest 88 rollouts 94.3 % accuracy, 0 false positives, every failure type caught; the remaining errors are recordings that end after the operator reset adopted (G9c-3) Robometer-4B zero-shot ArmnetBench, 2 099 rollouts, 7 policies pooled AUROC 0.818; episode length alone 0.938 fail Robometer-4B zero-shot own rollouts AUROC 0.58–0.62 fail Gemini Flash, sliding-window FAIL probability 50 episodes threshold fitted at 0.98: caught 0/8 failures, ~10 s per call fail Gemini Flash, two checkpoint calls (after grasp, at rest) 50 episodes flags 41/42 successes fail NVIDIA Flora-Rewarder-27B, 64-frame side-by-side clip, terminal prompt 50 episodes 8/8 failures, 2/42 successes, AUROC 1.00, deterministic, 6 s per episode pass Same input, Flora's base model Qwen3.5-27B, no robot fine-tune 50 episodes 7/8, 2/42, AUROC 0.91 pass Same input, Qwen3.5-9B 50 episodes 16/42 successes flagged fail Same input, Gemini Flash (64 JPEGs) 50 episodes 8/8, 3/42, AUROC 0.96 narrow fail

Reading. The fine-tune was not what made Flora work on this task; a whole-episode clip with both cameras and a terminal outcome question did, and only models of ~27B and up answer it well. Sliding windows and single checkpoints fail on the same episodes because nested bowls and partial lifts are ambiguous mid-episode. Two cheap baselines (episode length, policy identity) beat two published judges out of the box; they are computed first in every protocol here.

docs.title: 3. Small VLAs on a $300 arm: the bottleneck is the engine, not the model
docs.text:
Question. Which policy, which inference path, and what does it cost?

Policy Machine Success (10 trials) Chunk inference ACT Orin NX 9/10 59 ms SmolVLA 450M, PyTorch Orin NX 9/10 974 ms SmolVLA 450M, vla.cpp Orin NX 9/10 390 ms SmolVLA 450M, vla.cpp + flash attention Orin NX 8/10 238 ms VLA-JEPA (Qwen3-VL-2B + DiT-B), fine-tuned for $9.7 Orin NX 9/10 355 ms TurboVLA Orin NX 0/3 closed: ignores the instruction (task-distinguishing frames were 6 % of the data)

Reading. On a single-task benchmark all three working policies hit the ceiling; the task cannot separate them, and the 2B model costs 3× the training budget of the 450M one for the same score. The real gains came from the loop: vla.cpp cut SmolVLA's latency 4×, and a gradient-free prefix overwrite at chunk boundaries (ported into vla.cpp, +0.4 ms) cuts the median boundary jump by 72–74 %, where exact RTC guidance manages 21–41 % at twice the latency. 24 % of failed episodes show pose oscillation (REKI's metric), which is what the register-token port targets next.

docs.title: What is running now
docs.text: Architecture v1.5: an execution harness where a coding agent (Claude Code over MCP tools) dispatches unit actions to a small VLA, verifies at rest through a per-task verifier slot, logs every trial, and turns verified rollouts into the next fine-tuning set and the next list of teleops to record. The world model runs in shadow mode. Current task: a LEGO-kitting cell (pick bricks from bulk into a carousel, verify by scale), chosen because it is a product and not a labour cost. Details in Architecture.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: SO-101 follower + leader (teleop), Logitech C920 top camera (oblique), wrist camera, Jetson Orin NX 16 GB Super (headless, Docker image published), MacBook for offline evaluation, vast.ai for training (ranked by whole-job cost: GPU + disk + bandwidth). Nothing in the control loop larger than a 450M policy and a 192-d world model; everything bigger runs off-board.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Fifteen versions in three weeks, each one forced by a gate result. The current design is v1.5. The short version: the robot station is a harness; a coding agent is its operator; scripted motions and a small VLA are interchangeable executors; the verifier is a per-task plugin with a stated credibility tier; every trial, whoever dispatched it, is a labelled record that feeds the next fine-tune and the next teleop session.

Status

v1.5 is specified and partly built (harness code with 284 tests, first LEGO teleop session: 60 episodes). It has not run end-to-end on the arm yet. Everything on the results page comes from v0.8–v1.1 gates.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
do_action(action, executor="auto", key=(run, action_id, attempt))
  → { trial_id, executor_status, verdict, verifier_evidence, budgets_left }

executor_status ∈ { done, timeout, clamped, error }        # what the motion did
verdict         ∈ { satisfied, violated, ambiguous, stale } # what the verifier says
ok              := executor_status == done and verdict == satisfied
  • Two fields, never one. The executor never writes the verdict; the verifier never reads the agent's text or the plan. ambiguous (scale unstable, mask count disagrees) and stale (observation older than the last motion) are first-class and can only lead to a budgeted re-observe, never to success.
  • Idempotent dispatch. The same key twice returns the same trial record. This closes "the agent retried after a lost tool response and the arm picked twice".
  • Budgets the agent cannot raise. Per-class counters (re-observe, undo, refill pause, executor switch); exhausting one opens a ticket to the agent, then to the owner.

docs.title: The verifier is a plugin slot with credibility tiers
docs.text:
Verifier(context, trial) → { verdict, evidence, tier }
tier 1  physical measurement        scale, count, limit switch
tier 2  deterministic perception    mask count, colour, pose at rest   (bowls: the G9c-3 judge, 0 false positives)
tier 3  learned / VLM judge         Robometer, VLM on before/after clips
tier 4  owner label                 ground truth, slow

Tiers 1–2 can pass a reliability gate and admit trials to demos/ on their own. Tier 3 only pairs with a tier-2 verdict, and only after a verifier report card (false positives and negatives against owner labels on that task) exists. This rule comes directly from the gates: the sliding-window VLM judge caught 0/8 failures, the checkpoint judge flagged 41/42 successes, Robometer scored 0.58 zero-shot. A learned verifier earns its place per task, never by default. Fine-tuning a policy on tier-3 demos without a spot-check trains it on the judge's mistakes.

docs.title: The data flywheel
docs.text: Every trial is written in LeRobot v3 with task_string, layout_id, executor and version, verdict and evidence. demos/ is a view: satisfied trials from tier-1/2 verifiers. The next teleop session is planned from the log: failed layouts first (at most a third of the budget), then farthest-point coverage of the workspace. A policy is adopted for a skill only through G24: enough verified demos covering the failing skill, a verification window with scripted fallback, per-call finish rate not below the incumbent, kit success not dropping; otherwise revert. Every "prefer executor X for Y" note is versioned and marked unverified after a policy swap.

docs.title: Where the world model sits
docs.text: Shadow mode. W1 scores every trial (outcome readout, surprise trace) and the scores are logged next to the verdict, because G10 showed it reads outcomes perfectly and the screening gates showed it does not yet anticipate them reliably. It becomes an active veto only if a fresh-rollout gate passes against the joint-only baseline. Candidate gate: object-state and contact events (G7), where the commanded joints are blind.

docs.title: Three decisions that shaped it
docs.text:
1. Verify at rest, not mid-motion. Six mid-episode verifiers (stage trackers from proprio, masks and latents; sliding-window and checkpoint VLM judges; world-model reflexes) failed their gates on the same day. One deterministic judge at rest with 0 false positives passed. Everything downstream is built around that asymmetry.
  2. The agent stays out of the motion loop. Claude Code dispatches unit actions and batches, handles tickets, plans the next session, and edits tools under a check. It never sits inside a 33 ms tick (HexaShell's 739 s of agent time for 26 s of robot time is the cautionary number).
  3. A task is a plugin. Catalogue, planner, perception config, verifier and task gates are the only things that change between bowls, bricks and whatever comes next. The harness, the logging schema and the adoption protocol do not.

docs.text:
Every gate, in date order. Bar is the pass rule written down before the run; Result is what was measured; Verdict applies the bar and nothing else. A row is never rewritten to fit a later result; corrections are added as new rows (see G9a-AB, G11-A, G12). Costs are vast.ai invoices where they exist.

Method

Pre-register the rule, compute the cheap baseline first (episode length, policy identity, commanded joints), run the experiment only if one of its outcomes changes the next decision, and label anything decided after the number as exploratory. This is what kept the negative results below trustworthy.

docs.title: Lessons the numbers paid for
docs.text:
1. A world model that predicts well can still be useless for choosing actions. Prediction quality is not decision quality.
  2. On a position-controlled arm, the commanded joints already say where the arm will be. Test the world model on object state and contact, not on arm motion.
  3. Raw latent distance is not progress. A progress signal has to be trained on progress labels.
  4. Spatial features beat a single pooled vector (W1 pose R² 0.57 vs W2 0.92). Never PCA-compress the latent.
  5. Judging is easier than imagining, but zero-shot judges are not free either: compute episode length and policy identity before any model.
  6. Top-1 of N compounds errors (top-1 ≈ pairwise^7). Use regret.
  7. Missing data isn't random: 22 % of episodes lost to one OOM were two whole tasks, and re-scoring them flipped the verdict.
  8. Idle frames teach freezing; instruction-dependent behaviour needs data where the instruction matters.
  9. Freeze the rule before the number. It is what makes the failures above worth publishing.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware
docs.text:
One post per paper I have run against the SO-101 / Orin setup. Each post has the same shape: what the paper claims and how it measures it (protocol, n, baselines), what I ran with the gate ID, their number beside mine, what the gap means, a one-line verdict, and what would change it. The gates are in the experiment log; the long-form reading of every paper is in the private repo's journal/book/ and is being folded in here as each experiment runs.

Verdict words are the register's: reproduces (their claim holds here within the bar), fail (the pre-registered bar was not met and the confound checklist is clean), not proven (bar not met, a confound is open), not tested (no run that tests the paper's claim yet).

docs.title: Posts
docs.text: The work in the order it happened, one post per phase: contributions, experiments and negative results. Each number links back to the experiment log; nothing was rewritten after the fact.

docs.title: LeRobot on a Jetson: why there is no pip install torch, and what it took
docs.text: pip install lerobot fails on a Jetson Orin with an error that says almost nothing. The cause: LeRobot needs Python ≥ 3.12 and torchcodec ≥ 0.11 on aarch64 with CUDA, and no channel (NVIDIA's redist, the community index) ships a cp312 CUDA torch wheel for Jetson. The fix is a Docker image that builds the stack from source; it is merged upstream as LeRobot #4599 and published on GHCR. This post is about the traps underneath it.

docs.title: Why not jetson-containers
docs.text: The usual answer is dusty-nv/jetson-containers. Its last human-merged PR was months old and its own issue thread says it is no longer maintained; its lerobot package lacks torchcodec, references a renamed extra and a CLI that no longer exists. Depending on it would mean waiting on a lane with zero throughput.

docs.title: Five things built from source
docs.text:
1. PyTorch 2.11 for cp312, TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.7.
  2. torchcodec 0.11 with CUDA, against a local NVDEC ffmpeg.
  3. torchvision 0.26.
  4. FFmpeg with --enable-cuda-nvcc --enable-nvdec --enable-cuvid.
  5. dav1d, because ffmpeg 8.1 wants a newer one than Ubuntu 22.04 ships.

docs.title: The traps
docs.text:
• PyTorch auto-enables NVSHMEM once USE_DISTRIBUTED=1 finds the nvidia-nvshmem pip package, and the link fails after five hours of compiling. USE_NVSHMEM=0, explicitly.
  • USE_FLASH_ATTENTION=0 is ignored if build/CMakeCache.txt exists from an earlier attempt; the parallel template-heavy kernels then OOM-kill a 16 GB board. Force it with cmake -DUSE_FLASH_ATTENTION=OFF ..
  • USE_DISTRIBUTED=0, the sensible choice for a single board, crashes lerobot-train: its is_main_process() calls torch.distributed.is_initialized() unconditionally, and the stub module has no such method. Build with distributed on and Gloo as the backend.
  • The PyPI torchvision installs and imports fine against a from-source torch and only fails on the first compiled op: operator torchvision::nms does not exist. Build it from source, matched.
  • ffmpeg's vendored NVENC code disagrees with the Video Codec SDK headers on a struct field. Decode only is needed, so drop NVENC; note that ./configure auto-enables it when headers are present and only --disable-nvenc is the off switch.
  • A dependency's install script swallows its own failure (|| echo FAILED without exit 1), so the Docker layer builds and the missing binary surfaces two stages later.

docs.title: The number to plan around
docs.text: Full build: 5 h 33 min, of which PyTorch alone is 92 %. Everything else is under 15 minutes.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Verified on an Orin NX 16 GB: torch.cuda.is_available(), a real .cuda() tensor out of torchcodec, torch.distributed.is_gloo_available(), import lerobot, a SmolVLA import. docker pull ghcr.io/ravediamond/lerobot-jetson:latest. Source and full build log: ravediamond/lerobot-jetson. The write-up reached about 49k people on LinkedIn, with a public thumbs-up from LeRobot's tech lead; it is also the image every Jetson gate on this site runs in.

docs.title: Three policies on a $300 arm, and a gate harness to compare them
docs.text: Before any research question, the arm had to run a learned policy reliably and I had to be able to measure it the same way every time. This post is the baseline everything else is compared against.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• SO-101 follower arm (6 DoF, STS3215 servos), SO-101 leader for teleop, Logitech C920 top camera, a wrist camera.
  • Jetson Orin NX 16 GB as the robot computer, headless, in a Docker image I published (the Dockerfile is merged upstream in LeRobot, #4599).
  • A MacBook M1 for a second machine, and vast.ai for anything that needs a real GPU.
  • Task: "put the blue bowl in the pink bowl", and the reverse. 182 teleop episodes, idle starts trimmed, public on the Hub as ravediamond/so101_bowls_all_trimmed.

docs.title: The harness
docs.text: monitor_rollout.py runs a fixed number of trials, logs a tick file per trial (joint commands, chunk latency, timestamps), records video from both cameras, and takes one key press from the operator at the end of each trial: success or failure. Every trial since this day sits in one catalogue, 85 of them with video by mid-October. The rule that mattered later: freeze the pass bar before the run.

docs.title: Results, 10 trials each
docs.text:
Policy Machine Success Chunk inference ACT M1 Mac 10/10 – SmolVLA 450M (PyTorch) M1 Mac 9/10 – ACT Orin NX 9/10 59 ms SmolVLA 450M (PyTorch) Orin NX 9/10 974 ms

Both policies work. SmolVLA at 974 ms per 50-action chunk is a problem on the Orin: the arm visibly pauses at every chunk boundary. That number is the reason the next post exists.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: The first thing a hobby setup needs is not a better model, it is a harness that produces the same number twice. Operator judgment is fine for 10 trials; it will not be fine for 100, which is a judging problem I only understood two weeks later.

docs.title: SmolVLA four times faster on the Jetson with vla.cpp
docs.text: 974 ms per chunk made SmolVLA stutter on the Orin NX. Serving the same checkpoint through vla.cpp brought it to 238 ms with no loss in task success.

docs.title: Numbers, same bowls task, 10 trials
docs.text:
Engine Success Chunk inference SmolVLA, PyTorch 9/10 974 ms SmolVLA, vla.cpp 9/10 390 ms SmolVLA, vla.cpp + flash attention 8/10 238 ms

The 8/10 on the flash-attention build is one failed trial out of ten; the gate is too small to say whether that is a regression or noise. Inference went from blocking the control loop most of the time to 14 % of the time at the 26.6 Hz tick.

docs.title: What it took
docs.text:
• A cppzmq workaround for Ubuntu 22.04 / JetPack 6, now documented upstream (vla.cpp #47).
  • Real SO-101 latency numbers posted on the project's benchmark issue (#31), which were the first on this hardware.
  • An --arch act client preset so the same client drives ACT and SmolVLA.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: On GPU-poor hardware the engine is the lever, not the model. Everything that follows runs the policy through vla.cpp, and two weeks later the same engine is where the chunk-boundary fix lands at a cost of 0.4 ms.

docs.title: Benchmarking twelve VLAs on an Orin NX for vla.cpp
docs.text: vla.cpp (the llama.cpp-style engine for vision-language-action models) had benchmark reports for the Orin Nano Super and the AGX Orin, and nothing in between. The Orin NX 16 GB is the board most hobby arms end up on. This report fills the gap and is merged upstream as vla.cpp #36.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text: The project's own template: 3 warm-ups, 20 repetitions, best of 3 processes, a flag screen, then a full re-run of the fastest flag set. JetPack 6.2, CUDA 12.6, MAXN_SUPER, built on the board with -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=87. Twelve of thirteen models; OpenVLA-OFT does not fit in memory. Every GGUF's sha256 checked against the Hub. One evening, 18:10 to 20:57, no errors.

docs.title: Headline, minimum ms per inference at the defaults
docs.text:
Octo TurboVLA VLA-JEPA GR00T N1.7 BitVLA SmolVLA π0 Evo-1 Orin Nano Super 31.9 89.3 193.9 271.7 335.0 462.8 845.2 1011.5 Orin NX 16 GB 27.4 79.7 176.7 251.4 269.1 411.2 739.6 893.2 AGX Orin 17.5 36.0 94.6 132.7 133.0 218.3 350.3 434.6

Every model lands between the two existing boards, as it should. The fastest flags match the Nano report except GR00T N1.6, where --weight-dtype f16 passes the 3 % rule on this board.

docs.title: Two things worth knowing
docs.text:
• On this L4T release, getrusage peak RSS does not include CUDA buffers (π0 reports 483 MiB here against 5 961 MiB on the Nano). I kept the template column as measured and added a whole-board tegrastats column with the idle baseline; the maintainer chose to drop the memory columns.
  • Throttling check: GPU clock stayed at 1 162–1 172 MHz, junction temperature ≤ 83 °C under the full sweep, so the numbers are not thermally capped.

docs.title: Why it matters here
docs.text: These are engine latencies on fixed inputs. The same board running SmolVLA on a real SO-101 through the full client measured 238–390 ms per chunk, which is the number the control loop actually sees. Both numbers are on the issue tracker (#31) so the next person with this board does not have to guess.

docs.title: TurboVLA: a policy that ignored its instruction
docs.text:
Ten days of work, several variants, a published PyPI package, and a closed project. TurboVLA fine-tuned on the two-task bowls data learned to perform whichever task it had seen last, whatever the instruction said. The failure taught me two things about data that the later datasets were built around.

Corrected 2026-10-23

The conclusion below about the model was wrong. My port differed from the paper in four places, and the paper's own trainer, run on the same data with the paper's initialisation, also ignores the instruction (task swap 0.020° vs 0.105 for the same model on LIBERO-Goal). The data finding (fact 7) is the whole story. Full account: Paper vs hardware 12: TurboVLA.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
• Checkpoint conversion from the LIBERO warm start worked (verified 2026-09-08).
  • Trained on bowls, it rolled out at 0/3 on the last variant. On inspection it did the same motion for "blue in pink" and "pink in blue": a copycat.
  • An upstream-port spec was written for the maintainers, and the honest estimate was about one chance in three of passing a 50-episode benchmark. I stopped.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
1. Instruction-dependent behaviour needs data where the instruction matters. In the bowls set, the frames where the two tasks differ (which bowl to grasp first) are about 6 % of all frames. The rest is identical reach, lift, place. A policy can fit 94 % of the data while ignoring the instruction entirely.
  2. Idle frames teach freezing. The earlier recordings started with the arm at rest for a second or two. TurboVLA learned "stay" as a valid action. Every dataset since has its idle starts trimmed with the same script.

docs.title: What survived
docs.text: lerobot-policy-turbovla-so101 stays on PyPI as a working plugin policy; the bowls dataset was re-cut; the two lessons went into the recording guide. Not every project needs to end in a merge to be worth the time.

docs.title: VLA-JEPA on the Orin for $9.7, and why best-of-N reranking is a no-go
docs.text: The first world-model idea was the obvious one: let the policy propose several action chunks, let a latent world model imagine each one, keep the best. Before building any of it, I checked whether the premise held. It did not.

docs.title: VLA-JEPA on the arm
docs.text: Fine-tuned on vast.ai for about $9.7 (over the $3.5–4.7 estimate: interruptible bids cost more than they save on long runs). On the Orin NX, world model off at inference: 9/10 on bowls, 355 ms per chunk. Same score as SmolVLA at three times the training cost. The task is at its ceiling and cannot tell them apart; that comparison waits for a harder primitive.

docs.title: H0: do the samples vary enough to pick from?
docs.text:
Pre-registered bars: oracle-to-mean error ratio ≤ 0.7, latency for 8 samples ≤ 1.5× one sample, baseline success below 85 %.

  • The 8 samples are bundled: 1.08° spread, oracle/mean ratio 0.76 (null 0.92).
  • Latency 1.84× (643 vs 349 ms).
  • Baseline success 90 %, already above the bar where reranking could pay.
  • Averaging the 8 chunks, with no model at all, captures 45 % of the oracle gain.

Verdict: no-go. A reranker cannot fix a bias the samples share, and the cheapest competitor (the mean) takes half the available gain for free.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text: Reranking left the architecture the same day. The question became whether a world model can see a failure, not whether it can choose an action. That turned out to be a much better question, with a much longer answer.

docs.title: A JEPA world model from pixels for $3.30
docs.text: LeWM (the stable-worldmodel recipe: a JEPA trained end to end from pixels, no reconstruction) on the 182 bowls episodes, two camera views, 100 epochs. Gate G0 asked whether the model is real before anything is built on it.

docs.title: Getting it to train
docs.text: Eleven setup problems between the paper's code and this data and hardware, on vast.ai x86 and on the Jetson GPU. $0.28 of smoke runs. A 5-epoch model reacted to gross action errors (episode swap, frozen action) but not to ±0.5 s timing shifts, and its latent had an effective rank of 5.8 out of 192: too short to judge.

docs.title: G0, the faithful run
docs.text:
Pre-registered bars: beat copy-last; every corruption ratio ≥ 1.3 at K = 30; no collapse.

  • Open-loop error at K = 30: 0.31 vs 0.89 for copy-last.
  • Timing shifts: ratios 1.99 and 1.58. The model uses the actions.
  • Effective rank 24–30. No collapse.
  • Linear probes on the latent: grasp onset AUROC 0.94, holding 0.995.
  • Cost: $3.30, plus $2.96 of failed attempts before it.

Pass. This model, called W1 from here on, is the one every later gate tests.

docs.title: C1, the first disappointment
docs.text: Does the imagined latent predict rollout failures better than the current one? On the 81 gate rollouts: current latent 0.68, imagined 0.72, and policy identity alone 0.76. Most failures came from TurboVLA, so "which policy ran" explains more than any latent. Not proven, confounded. The lesson that stuck: compute the cheap baseline before the model, every time.

docs.title: Porting ACT to vla.cpp, so a Jetson can run it without PyTorch
docs.text: ACT is the most common SO-101 policy and vla.cpp did not have it. Merged as vla.cpp #38 after a scoping issue (#37) the maintainer approved in a day. The pitch was never speed: PyTorch ACT already runs at 59 ms per 100-action chunk on the Orin. The pitch is no PyTorch at inference: no 5.5-hour source build, no 12–24 GB image, and CPU-only boards can run it.

docs.title: What a port involves
docs.text:
CONTRIBUTING.md lists the seven mechanical sites for a new architecture. Most of ACT's pieces already existed in-tree:

  • An ACT-style transformer decoder with learned queries, from the TurboVLA implementation.
  • Conv + group norm via im2col, from Octo. ACT's ResNet-18 uses frozen batch norm, which folds into the conv weights at conversion time.
  • No flow-matching steps: ACT goes on the num_steps refusal list. The VAE encoder is training-only, so the latent is zeros at inference.

The converter and act.cpp read state and action dims, camera count and resolution from the checkpoint config rather than hard-coding the SO-101, because the maintainer asked for a parity check on lerobot/act_aloha_sim_transfer_cube_human as well: bimanual, 14-dim, one 480×640 camera.

docs.title: How it was tested
docs.text:
• vla_predict_check against PyTorch on fixed inputs for both checkpoints (ours and the ALOHA one).
  • The same gate harness as every other policy here, with an --engine vlacpp path for ACT, on the real arm. The PyTorch checkpoint scores 9/10 on the Orin NX.
  • An --arch act client preset in the LeRobot-side client fork, so the same client drives ACT and SmolVLA (no tokenizer, ImageNet normalization).

docs.title: Why a hobby lab should do ports
docs.text: A port is the one contribution nobody can casually redo without your hardware, and it forces you to read the model as code rather than as a paper. The same reading is what later turned up a silently wrong objective in another policy's training code (LeRobot #4381) and the chunk-boundary fix that went into this engine a week after (G13b).

docs.title: The world model loses to the commanded joints
docs.text: G1b asked the question that decides whether a latent world model can plan on this arm: given the expert chunk and seven decoys, does imagining each one rank the expert first? Two world models, one bigger pretrained one, and a baseline with no model at all. The baseline won.

docs.title: G1b: plannable range
docs.text:
Bar: top-1 ≥ 0.8 at some target distance.

  • W1 (192-d, trained here): best 0.60 at d = 20–30. Fail.
  • W2 (frozen DINOv2-S patches + learned dynamics): arm-pose R² 0.92 vs W1's 0.57, so the representation is far better; on G1b, 0.55–0.61. Fail. A decision with W2 takes 1.8 s on the Mac anyway (G2), so a third, bigger model W3 was not run.
  • RoboJEPA (pretrained, V-JEPA 2.1 features): the encoder takes 526 ms for two views on the Orin NX and 1 025 ms on the Mac. Off the robot. Zero-shot on our latents, the 1B model is borderline on a partial sample and action conditioning does work on our arm (9–10 % below shuffled actions). Not enough to earn a role.

docs.title: The diagnosis
docs.text:
Top-1 among 8 compounds pairwise errors: W2's pairwise accuracy is 0.92–0.93, and 0.92^7 ≈ 0.56, which is exactly its top-1. A 0.8 top-1 bar needs ~97 % per comparison. Regret replaced top-1 as the metric.

Then the control: score chunks with the commanded joint trajectory alone, no images, no model. Top-1 0.68–0.90, regret ≈ 0. On a position-controlled arm, the actions already say where the arm will be. G1b was measuring kinematics, and the joints are a better kinematics model than any latent trained on 182 episodes.

docs.title: What it means
docs.text: A world model only has something to add where the actions are blind: object state, contact, failures. Prediction quality (G0 passed) is not decision quality (G1b failed). The next gates test exactly that boundary, and the planning role is gone for good.

docs.title: Latent distance is not progress
docs.text: If a world model cannot rank actions, maybe it can tell how far along a task is: distance in latent space to the goal frame should fall as the arm gets closer, and a stall is when it stops falling. Zero labels needed. G6a tested that; G6b tested a hierarchical version four days later. Both failed the same way.

docs.title: G6a
docs.text:
Bars: Spearman correlation between step and distance-to-goal ≤ −0.8 over successful demos; done-detector AUROC ≥ 0.95.

  • Monotonicity: −0.32 to −0.50 for every variant. The arm's trajectory loops in physical space (approach, lift, swing, place), so distance to the final frame rises and falls on the way there.
  • Stall rule derived from it: 32 % false stalls on held-out successes.
  • Done detector: AUROC 0.97–1.00, but its negatives were at-rest frames before any grasp. An easy contrast proves little.

docs.title: G6b: the hierarchy
docs.text: H-JEPA's level-2 slow features (coarse stride 15, SIGReg loss) were supposed to smooth the loops out. Monotonicity −0.73 against a −0.80 bar; 52 % false stalls. The hierarchy was dropped, and with it the last planning-shaped role in the stack.

docs.title: What the papers already said
docs.text: TD-JEPA reports ~0.65 for raw latent distance against 0.95 for a learned cost; the Planning-Limits paper shows rollouts shorter than the target distance rank below chance even with a perfect simulator. I had read both. Running the gate anyway cost nothing on the Mac and turned "the papers say" into "on this arm, this number". A progress signal has to be trained on progress labels; nothing here produced one for free.

docs.title: Judging a rollout: the zero-false-positive rule
docs.text: Ten operator-judged trials are fine. An autonomous loop that records hundreds of rollouts and fine-tunes on the good ones is not, because every success it mislabels trains the policy on a failure. This is the day the judge became the most important component in the stack, and the day a published 4B reward model lost to 40 lines of OpenCV.

docs.title: Robometer-4B, zero-shot
docs.text:
On ArmnetBench (2 099 SO-101 rollouts, 7 policies), a first run on the partial set gave a qualified pass at AUROC 0.861. Re-scoring the 462 episodes lost to one CUDA OOM (two whole tasks, the longest episodes) brought the complete set to 0.818: fail. Episode length alone scores 0.938. Missing data is not random, and a partial result is provisional until it covers every task.

On our own 88 rollouts: AUROC 0.58–0.62. The main failure mode (grasping the wrong bowl) is an object-identity question that a trajectory-comparison reward model has no reason to answer.

docs.title: G9c: a deterministic judge
docs.text:
Top camera, HSV masks for the two bowls, centroid geometry: is the blue blob inside the pink one at the end? No learning.

Version End rule Accuracy False positives G9c last frame 86.4 % 0 G9c-2 arm back at rest 29/88 invalid (failing policies rarely return to rest) 0 G9c-3 stillness or timeout 94.3 % 0

All twelve G9c errors are successes whose recording continues past the operator's reset, so the final frame shows the bowls separated again. Judged at the marked reset instead: 95.5 %. G9c-3 misses its pre-registered 95 % bar by 0.7 points and is adopted anyway, because the one number that matters for a training loop is the false-positive count, and it is zero.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text: A judge that never calls a failure a success can be slow, narrow and dumb. One that does, however clever, poisons the data. Everything later (the verifier tiers in v1.5) comes from this table.

docs.title: What the world model is actually for
docs.text: With a judge that is right at rest, the world model finally had a fair question: can it read the judge's verdict from the latent, and can it see it coming? G10 ran on the Mac for free. It is the one world-model gate that passed cleanly, and the next post is about how much of it survived contact with fresh data.

docs.title: G10
docs.text:
Bars: outcome readout at the judge's timestamp AUROC ≥ 0.90; anticipation 30 steps earlier must beat policy identity by +0.10.

  • Step 1, readout at t_j: W1 AUROC 1.000, W2 0.976. The latent at rest contains the outcome.
  • Step 2, anticipation at t_j − 30: the imagined latent beats policy identity by +0.179 (0.993 against ground truth).
  • Mid-chunk surprise (prediction error of the next latent): 1.82× higher on missed grasps, 2.58× on stalls, from the first step.

Pass. The architecture of record changed the same day: no planning, no progress tracking. The world model is a pre-execution veto (imagine the chunk, refuse it if the imagined outcome reads as failure) and a mid-chunk surprise monitor.

docs.title: G11-A: does it fit in the tick?
docs.text:
Dual-camera surprise check on the Orin NX, FP16 CUDA: 12.78 ms mean, 12.95 ms max, inside a 33 ms control tick with 20 ms to spare. Pass.

A correction row was added the next day: the benchmark had loaded the checkpoint with strict=False and a key remap that did not fit the image's transformers version, so its encoder was random. The timing stands (same architecture); the latent values from that run are void. A strict-load check now runs before every Jetson gate.

docs.title: Honest reading, written before the next gates
docs.text: G10 is retrospective: W1 was scored on the same 69 rollouts it had seen as unlabeled training video. The real test is a fresh rollout and a fixed threshold. That test came two days later.

docs.title: Verify at rest: six mid-episode monitors fail in one day
docs.text: One Jetson day, no arm motion, every mid-episode verifier in the v1.0 design run against 50 fresh rollouts with the bars frozen the night before. Stage trackers, VLM judges and the world-model reflex all failed. One offline engine experiment passed. The architecture that came out of it (v1.1) verifies only at rest, and that rule has not moved since.

docs.title: The world model, on fresh data
docs.text:
Test Bar Result W1-A: L2 surprise, cosine drift, live reflex (2.2 / 10.0) as screeners one signal catches ≥ 5/8 failures at ≤ 1/20 false interventions L2 2/8 (AUROC 0.86); drift 0/8; the live reflex fires on 42/42 successes G11-B-cal: refit the reflex from episode maxima recall ≥ 50 % on 25 failures 3/25 at 1/44 false alarms; success and failure maxima overlap W1-C1: event-anchored grasp check from the imagined latent AUROC ≥ 0.85, ≥ 0.05 above the current latent imagined 0.70, current 0.82: imagination is worse W1-C2: conformal band on the surprise trace (FAIL-Detect / SAFE) successes flagged ≤ 1/20, failures ≥ 50 % 22.7 % / 46 %; the band is not conformal across time when μ and σ are fit on the same successes

G10's thresholds did not transfer. The world model went to shadow mode: scored and logged on every trial, never allowed to stop the arm.

docs.title: Stage trackers and VLM judges
docs.text:
• G15 (proprio + masks): 48 % premature, 47 % missed. The gripper reads 1.1° when holding a bowl rim, below every "closed on nothing" threshold, so a grasp detector built on aperture cannot fire.
  • G15-v2 and the latent-prototype tracker W1-B: unusable on this gripper; 22 % / 31 %.
  • Gemini Flash with sliding-window FAIL probability: threshold fitted at 0.98, 0/8 failures caught, 10 s per call.
  • Gemini Flash with two checkpoint calls (after grasp, at rest): 41/42 successes flagged. Nested bowls read as "blue alone on the mat"; the post-grasp checkpoint comes before the lift.

docs.title: The one that passed: G13b
docs.text: Chunk boundaries are where SmolVLA jerks. Real-time chunking (RTC) does inference-time guidance; the gradient-free alternative overwrites the new chunk's prefix with the tail of the old one. On 20 episodes, 254 boundaries: prefix overwrite cuts the median boundary jump 72–74 %; exact RTC 21–41 % at twice the latency. Ported into vla.cpp the same day: 71–73 %, prefix error 0.0, +0.4 ms per chunk, default path bit-identical, 14/14 tests.

docs.title: v1.1
docs.text: Verification and repair at rest with the deterministic judge; prefix overwrite in the engine; world model in shadow mode; every trial recorded. The simplest design of the series, and the first one forced entirely by its own negative results.

docs.title: Judging, part 2: the input format did the work
docs.text: The deterministic judge is right but narrow: it knows about two coloured bowls. Any new task needs a judge that reads video. NVIDIA's Flora-Rewarder-27B, a robot-trained outcome scorer, passed where Gemini had failed the day before. The ablation says why, and it is not the robot training.

docs.title: G-flora
docs.text:
Input exactly as NVIDIA's terminal prompt expects: 64 frames, top and wrist camera side by side, no telemetry, greedy decoding. 50 episodes, 42 successes and 8 failures, bar frozen before any call: at the largest score threshold flagging ≤ 2/42 successes, ≥ 6/8 failures must be flagged.

  • 8/8 failures, 2/42 successes, AUROC 1.00. Successes score 4–5, failures 1–3, including both wrong-object cases and both nested-bowl successes that fooled Gemini.
  • Deterministic (5/5 identical), 0 unparseable, 6 s per episode on an A100, $0.70 total.

Flora's licence is non-commercial, so it is evidence, not a component.

docs.title: G-flora-abl: fine-tune or format?
docs.text:
Same clip, same prompt, three general models.

Model Successes flagged Failures flagged AUROC Verdict Qwen3.5-27B (Flora's base, no robot fine-tune) 2/42 7/8 0.91 pass Qwen3.5-9B 16/42 – 0.75 fail Gemini 3.8 Flash, 64 JPEGs 3/42 8/8 0.96 narrow fail

Flora's base model, untouched, passes the same bar. The 9B does not. Gemini, which caught 0/8 with sliding windows the day before, catches 8/8 with the whole episode and a terminal question. The fine-tune added a little; the input format (whole episode, both views, one outcome question at the end) and model size did the work.

docs.title: What goes into the stack
docs.text: A commercial rewarder fine-tuned from Qwen3.5 on own labels is the planned tier-3 verifier. It pairs with the deterministic judge, never replaces it, and it gets a report card (false positives and negatives against owner labels) on every new task before any of its verdicts enter a training set. That rule is written into v1.5.

docs.title: v1.5: the station as a harness for a coding agent
docs.text: Three weeks of gates reduced the world-model stack to a verifier and a shadow signal. What remained was the actual bottleneck of a one-person robotics lab: deciding what to record next, running trials unattended, and keeping the training data clean. v1.5 is that loop, specified from nine recent papers on agent harnesses and self-improvement, and partly built. It has not run end to end on the arm yet; this post is a design note, not a result.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
Claude Code (operator) ── skills: use-case brief, station-session, failure-review
        │ MCP
Run layer       journal, budgets per failure class, resume, full trace
Harness tools   observe · do_action · run_batch · run_policy · undo · tickets · estop
Executors       scripted_pick_place | run_policy (SmolVLA 450M via vla.cpp)
Task plugin     catalogue · planner · perception · VERIFIER (tiered) · gates
Robot           SO-101 · cameras · scale · Jetson Orin NX · W1 in shadow mode

The agent dispatches unit actions and batches; it never sits inside the 33 ms tick (HexaShell's 739 s of agent time for 26 s of robot time is the number to avoid). A new task is a plugin: catalogue, planner, perception config, verifier, gates. The harness and the logging schema do not change.

docs.title: Three contracts
docs.text:
1. Two-field results. executor_status (done / timeout / clamped / error) and verdict (satisfied / violated / ambiguous / stale) are separate; ok is their conjunction. The executor never writes the verdict, the verifier never reads the agent's text. ambiguous can only lead to a budgeted re-observe.
  2. Idempotent dispatch. Every call carries (run, action_id, attempt); a repeat returns the existing trial. This closes "the agent retried after a lost tool response and the arm picked twice".
  3. Verifier tiers. 1 physical measurement (a scale, a count), 2 deterministic perception at rest (the G9c-3 judge), 3 learned or VLM judge, 4 owner label. Tiers 1–2 can pass a gate and admit trials to demos/ alone. Tier 3 only pairs with tier 2, and only after a report card on that task. The gate on tier 3 is the 10-19 and 10-20 results written as policy.

docs.title: The flywheel
docs.text: Every trial is a LeRobot v3 record with task string, layout id, executor and version, verdict and evidence. demos/ is a view over satisfied trials from tier-1/2 verifiers. The next teleop session is planned from the log: failed layouts first, at most a third of the budget, then farthest-point coverage of the workspace. A policy replaces a scripted executor only through an adoption protocol (G24): enough verified demos on the failing skill, a verification window with scripted fallback, per-call finish rate not below the incumbent, revert otherwise.

docs.title: First task
docs.text: LEGO kitting: pick bricks from bulk into a carousel, verify by weight. Chosen because it has a tier-1 verifier for free, and because a slow robot only caps volume on a product, where it would lose outright on a service. First teleop session: 60 episodes; harness code: 284 tests. The gates for it (H1, G22, K1, G24) are frozen and waiting for the arm.

docs.title: Two gates I voided, and the two-line check that would have caught them
docs.text: On 2026-10-18 two Jetson gates went into the register with bars frozen beforehand: G11-A passed, G12 failed. Both were voided the same day. G11-A timed the right model with the wrong weights; G12 timed the wrong model. Neither was a training or hardware problem. Both were caught by checking what the script had actually loaded.

docs.title: G11-A: 12.78 ms of a random encoder
docs.text:
G11 Phase A asked whether W1, the multi-view JEPA world model, can run its surprise check inside the 33.3 ms control tick on the Orin NX, motors off. Bar: under 20 ms per check. Result: mean 12.78 ms, p95 12.87, max 12.95. Pass, 20.5 ms of headroom.

The next Jetson run was meant to measure W1's error on a still scene. No camera was attached, so only the checkpoint load could run, through the live loader, which refuses strict=False. It failed: 192 missing keys, 192 unexpected, all in the ViT encoder.

The checkpoint was saved under transformers 5.19.0, which names ViT layers encoder.layers.N.attention.q_proj.*. The Docker image ships 5.5.4, which names the same tensor encoder.encoder.layer.N.attention.attention.query.*. A key remap renamed layers → layer and q_proj → attention.query, but did not add the inner encoder. level, so the remapped keys still missed. Under 5.19.0 all 279 checkpoint keys load verbatim, no remap.

G11-A's benchmark used the same remap with strict=False. All 192 encoder tensors stayed at random initialisation. The timing stands, since the architecture and compute are the same, but no latent and no surprise value from that script came from the trained encoder. The unit tests passed throughout: they only exercised the layers → layer rename on a stand-in model.

Register: timing valid, latents void.

docs.title: G12: parts that don't sum
docs.text:
G12 asked whether REKI, a 2.4B VLA with register-token memory, fits the Orin: memory ≤ 8 GB, chunk ≤ 250 ms. Result: 3.46 GB, 318.2 ms. Fail, and a decision to port the registers into SmolVLA instead.

Re-reading the report: 135.4 + 230.3 is not 318.2. The expert time came from a separate loop. Then the benchmark itself: a randomly initialised Qwen2.5-1.5B, text only, 256 random tokens, no vision tower, none of Qwen3.5's Gated DeltaNet layers, followed by a hand-written random expert, in eager PyTorch. And 3.46 GB matches that 1.64B-parameter proxy, not REKI's 2.4B. So 318 ms is neither REKI's latency on the Orin nor a bound on it.

Register: G12 void; REKI on the Orin is unmeasured.

docs.title: The two-line check
docs.text:
m = W1LiveMonitor.from_checkpoint(ckpt)  # load_state_dict(strict=True), never strict=False
assert set(m.model.state_dict()) == set(torch.load(ckpt, map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)["state_dict"])

The first line raises on any missing or unexpected key. The second confirms the checkpoint's keys were used verbatim, not through a remap that happened to fit. On G11-A's setup the first line stops at 192 keys before a single timing is taken.

docs.title: Parts must sum
docs.text: G12's check is arithmetic. If a report splits a latency into parts, the parts add up to the total, measured in the same loop. And the thing measured must be the thing named: parameter count, vision tower, layer types. A 2.4B model that peaks at the memory of a 1.64B one is a second sum that does not hold.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
Both gates had frozen bars, and both results were real measurements of something. Pre-registration stops the bar from moving after the number; it says nothing about what produced the number. So the checks now come before the number: a strict load with a key-set comparison for any checkpoint, and a sum over the parts for any latency breakdown.

G11-A's 12.78 ms survives. G12 is open again: the REKI decision now rests on the G14 oscillation audit and on a real measurement, with the vision tower and the real expert.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 6: ContactGuard
docs.text: ContactGuard (Zheng, Johnson-Roberson, Zhi; arXiv 2608.13438) is the closest paper to what I run: a LeWM-style world model used as a pre-contact failure monitor on a real arm. Their monitor works. Mine, built to the same protocol, does not, with the opposite sign.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
Shared ViT-tiny per camera, mean-pool three views then a linear projection → one latent; predictor of four AdaLN-zero blocks; LeWM loss trained teacher-forced on unlabelled rollouts and teleop; then frozen. The probe: anchor 15 frames (0.5 s) before the first gripper-closure command, roll out K = 30 steps under the policy's actual chunk, standardise the imagined latent, fit a class-balanced ℓ2 logistic regression on ~250 labelled grasp attempts per task, freeze one threshold per task on validation. Online: trigger on the first open→close in the upcoming chunk, abort before contact if P(fail) > τ.

Evaluation on an AgileX Piper with an ACT policy, four grasp settings, test episodes excluded from everything. Closed loop: 50 monitored live rollouts per setting with a 5-s pause-and-resume so the would-be outcome is recorded; AUC 0.99 / 0.95 / 0.90 / 0.92 vs a single-view LeWM and a no-rollout probe. Offline pools (n = 101–144, five seeded 5-fold CV): ContactGuard 0.98 vs current latent 0.84 — same encoder, labels, probe, pools, only the imagined future replaced by the present one — with paired bootstrap CIs excluding zero on every task. Action corruption (Table 3): shuffled chunks from other episodes collapse the full model from 0.965 to 0.535; zero and mean actions to ~0.84. So the signal is the specific action's imagined consequence. A counterfactual action swap raises P(fail) by +0.25 to +0.65. Proprioception added to the probe hurts on all four (small-data shortcut). Runtime 19 ms on a 5090.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
W1-C1 (2026-10-19). The protocol as written: anchor 15 frames before the first close, 30-step imagination under the executed chunk, logistic probe, current latent as the matched baseline, 5-fold × 5 seeds on the 69 published rollouts (65 scored; two stalls and two others never close). Bar: AUROC ≥ 0.85 and ≥ 0.05 above the current latent. Result: imagined 0.70 (folds 0.72 ± 0.13), current 0.82 (0.83 ± 0.11). Imagination is 0.12 worse. The fold threshold gives 27 % held-out false aborts.

W1 itself follows the multi-view ContactGuard recipe (mean-pooled views), which is why the comparison is as direct as it gets.

docs.title: Their number, my number
docs.text: Paper (Piper, ACT) This arm (SO-101, mixed policies) Imagined-latent probe 0.98 0.70 Current-latent probe 0.84 0.82 Difference +0.14, CI excludes 0 −0.12 Labelled attempts ~250 per task 65 Views 3 2 World-model training data rollouts + teleop teleop only Arm torque-controlled position-controlled servos

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
The current-latent probes agree (0.84 vs 0.82): the encoder reads "this state looks risky" about as well on both arms. The imagined-latent probes do not: theirs adds information, mine subtracts it. The candidates, none proven: their world model saw the deployed policy's own rollouts in training and mine saw only teleop, so my imagination is off-distribution exactly at the states the monitor is for; 65 labels vs 250; two views vs three; and a torque-controlled approach that carries contact information a position-controlled one does not. The paper gives the control that would say which: Table 3's action corruption. If shuffled chunks do not push my imagined-latent AUROC below 0.70, the rollout carries no action information on my data and the encoder, not the probe, is the gap. That test is offline and free and is now in the amendments.

Verdict: does not reproduce; the matched baseline wins on my arm; mechanism unknown.

What would change it: the corruption test, then W1 retrained with policy rollouts in the mix.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 5: D-JEPA
docs.text: D-JEPA (Liu, Wu, Wen, You, Zhang, Hao, Lin, Su; arXiv 2609.24749) names my strongest negative result — latent distance misorders the few candidates that compete for execution — and proposes a fix. I ran the fix with the wrong labels. This post says what the paper's test needs and why mine was not it.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
The "decision-local prediction gap": a world model's latent geometry can be globally informative (Spearman 0.90 between predicted and realised cost over all 63 candidates on a Push-T start) and still misorder the top four (0.11). The fix is not a training loss. It is a permutation-equivariant set operator over the whole candidate set: per candidate, a descriptor from the terminal latent minus the goal and its native rank; a shared encoder, two Set-Transformer layers, and a bounded correction δ = ε·tanh(·) with ε = 0.2, so the operator can only reorder within 2ε of the native minimum and can never overturn a confident choice (Prop. 2). Loss: success mass under a softmax over scores, a local ordering term near the boundary, and a trust penalty on unnecessary correction.

The supervision is the expensive part: every candidate in the set is executed from the restored start and labelled — counterfactual execution. Evaluation: Push-T confirmation cohort of 256 starts (Reacher 128, Granular 64) with fitting, calibration and evaluation starts disjoint, Wilson intervals in the figures, paired counts; Push-T 83.6 → 87.9, Reacher 86.7 → 93.8. Real PiPER with a V-JEPA 2-AC planner, 50 paired starts per task: Push-T 56 → 74, two-cube stack 72 → 88 (gains/losses 12/3 and 10/2).

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
W1-R (2026-10-22). The operator exactly as App. A.2 describes it, on frozen W1's G1b candidates, five seeds, τ calibrated on 20 % of training episodes. Labels: proxy — the executed expert chunk marked success, the seven decoys marked failure. Bar: mean regret ≤ 0.10 and ≤ action-only + 0.05. Result: W1-R regret 0.2631 vs W1 0.2630; the gate chose "never replace" in 24 of 25 operators because W1 ranks its own training episodes at 0.67–0.91 and validation at 0.45–0.61, so calibration found nothing to fix. An exploratory perfect rank-2 swap would reach 0.115–0.154: the bar is out of reach for a rank-local operator with K = 8 even with perfect labels.

An earlier draft of the angle (NEXT_ANGLES §1) described D-JEPA as a loss term on the world model. Claude Code caught the error when the protocol had to cite the section; the implementation is the operator, the write-up says plainly that it does not test the paper's claim.

docs.title: Their number, my number
docs.text: Paper This arm Labels executed outcomes of every candidate proxy: expert = success, decoys = failure Candidate set 63 (sim), planner's pool (real) 8 Fit / calibration / eval disjoint starts, Wilson CIs train / 20 % cal / held-out episodes Gain +4 to +17 points 0.000 regret

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
Nothing about D-JEPA was tested. Proxy labels are a tautology for the operator (the "success" is whichever candidate the expert took), so the operator has nothing to learn that the native rank does not already express. The paper's claim needs the labels the paper pays for: the outcome of actually executing each candidate from the same start. On my arm that is affordable only in one place — the G7 cube session, where the undo primitive restores the layout and G9c-3 labels at rest; four to eight executed candidates per start for a subset of starts is two hours of a robot day. The bounded-correction design, independently of the result, is the right safety property for any re-ranker on a physical arm.

Verdict: not tested; the proxy version fails and is renamed. The paper's protocol is written into the amendments for G7.

What would change it: executed outcomes on ≥ 25 held-out starts.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 2: DINO-WM
docs.text: DINO-WM (Zhou, Pan, LeCun, Pinto; arXiv 2411.04983) is the recipe behind W2: frozen DINOv2 patches plus a learned dynamics model. It had the better representation and lost the same planning gate as W1, more slowly.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
Three parts, one trained: a frozen DINOv2 encoder gives N patch embeddings per 224×224 frame; a ViT transition model takes H frames of patches with the action MLP-embedded and concatenated to every patch, attends causally at the frame level, and predicts the whole next frame of patches at once; a transposed-conv decoder trained separately is for visualisation only (backpropagating its loss into the predictor hurt, their A.4.3). Loss: ‖p(enc(o), φ(a)) − enc(o_{t+1})‖², teacher-forced. Because the encoder is frozen, collapse is impossible by construction; the price is a representation that cannot adapt to the task. Planning: CEM in MPC to an image goal, cost ‖ẑ_T − z_g‖²; gradient descent through the model was tried and was worse (A.5.3).

Six simulated environments. Metric: success on 50 sampled (start, goal) pairs (Chamfer distance on 10 instances for the deformable ones). Table 1: Push-T 0.90 vs DreamerV3 0.30, IRIS 0.32, TD-MPC2 0.00. Table 2, the number that matters most for anyone picking a representation: Push-T with DINO CLS 0.44, ResNet 0.20, R3M 0.42, DINO patches 0.90. No standard errors, no real robot, no non-learned baseline.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
W2: frozen DINOv2-S patches, learned dynamics, trained on the same 182 episodes. Lost to a disk failure; W2′ retrained on 2026-10-23 (seed 3073, $0.65) reproduces its probes exactly.

G1 probes. Arm-pose R² 0.92 (W1: 0.57), gripper-open AUROC 0.999, grasp onset 0.995. The frozen patch representation encodes the arm far better than W1's end-to-end CLS latent, which is Table 2's CLS-vs-patch result on real frames.

G1b, ranking. Bar: top-1 ≥ 0.8. Result: 0.55–0.61 at every horizon. Fail. Open-loop error 0.62 of copy-last (W1: 0.36) — the better representation came with worse dynamics; action-corruption ratio only 1.13 (reacts less to wrong actions than W1).

G2, latency. A single decision (10 rollouts × 30 steps) on the Mac: W1 108 ms, W2 1 814 ms. The DINOv2 encoder alone is hundreds of ms per frame on an Orin. W3 (bigger) was not run because the decision rule said it would not change the build.

G10 outcome readout. AUROC 0.976 (W1 1.000).

docs.title: Their number, my number
docs.text: Paper (sim) This arm Patch > CLS for state 0.90 vs 0.44 (Push-T success) R² 0.92 vs 0.57 (arm pose) Planning success 0.90 Push-T top-1 0.55–0.61; no-model baseline 0.68–0.90 Planning time 47 s/episode (LeWM's measurement) 1.8 s per decision on a Mac; off the Orin Pairwise accuracy not reported 0.92–0.93; top-1 ≈ pairwise⁷

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
The representation result transfers and the planning result does not, for the same reason as W1: nothing in the paper is compared to a planner with no model. The one new thing W2 taught: a better frozen encoder does not give better dynamics for free; the learned predictor on top of DINOv2 patches reacted less to wrong actions than the small end-to-end model. And DINO-WM-style online planning is off the table on an Orin on latency alone; the role is offline ranking or verification, where W2′'s patch tokens are the ones to use for anything object-level (G7).

Verdict: representation reproduces; planning fails the baseline; the encoder cost rules out the loop.

What would change it: an object-state test (G7) where the patch representation's spatial detail is the thing being measured, scored offline.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 7: FAIL-Detect and SAFE
docs.text: Two papers, one experiment: both calibrate a time-varying conformal band on successful rollouts and flag a run that leaves it. FAIL-Detect (Xu et al., TRI; arXiv 2503.08558) does it on learned OOD scores with no failure data; SAFE (Gu et al., UofT/TRI; arXiv 2506.09937) on a probe of the VLA's own features trained with failures. I ran the band on W1's surprise (W1-C2). It failed, and the way it failed is the way FAIL-Detect's own hardware section describes.

docs.title: What the papers claim, and how they measure it
docs.text:
FAIL-Detect: a scalar score per step from the policy's observation embedding — logpZO (a flow from the embedding distribution to N(0, I); the score is the log-density), NatPN, RND — plus post-hoc baselines (STAC, which needs 256 policy samples per step; PCA-kmeans; smoothness). A band over time is fitted to the success distribution; a flag is raised when the score exceeds it. Sixteen simulated settings (four robomimic tasks × two policies × ID/OOD); summary is top-1 count across settings: logpZO 10/16. Hardware: Franka bimanual, two tasks, fewer rollouts; logpZO top-1 on 8/12. The caveat is in §VI: with ID-only bands, OOD-but-successful rollouts are flagged, "at times yielding low or close to zero TNR"; the fix needs successes from every new setting. Detection time for STAC exceeds the average success duration.

SAFE: the VLA's last-layer features already separate success from failure across tasks (a shared "failure zone" in t-SNE). A tiny MLP or LSTM on them, trained on seen tasks with trajectory-level labels, generalises to unseen tasks. Threshold by functional conformal prediction on successful calibration rollouts, FPR ≤ α at any time step. Three random seen/unseen splits; ROC-AUC on the max-so-far score (a flag anywhere on a success is a false positive); 14 adapted baselines. Sim unseen AUROC ~0.78 vs best baseline ~0.74; real Franka 30 + 30 per task and WidowX 532 rollouts; < 1 ms overhead.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
W1-C2 (2026-10-19). A time-varying functional CP band on W1's long surprise, fitted on 22 successes, tested on the other 22 successes and the 8 failures, 20 seeds. Bar (median): successes flagged ≤ 1/20, failures ≥ 50 %. Result: successes 22.7 % (IQR 13.6–27.3), failures 46 %, stalls 34 %. Fail. The band as registered fits μ, σ and the radius on the same successes: on synthetic exchangeable data its false-alarm rate is 0.14 at 20 anchors — about α only with separate μ/σ data. So the band was not conformal across time as written, and even a correct band sits on a surprise distribution that widens on fresh data (W1-A: the live reflex fitted on one session flagged 42/42 successes on the next).

C1 probe (2026-10-11), the SAFE-shaped question — does the imagined latent predict failure better than simpler signals? — found policy identity alone at 0.76 beating every probe (current 0.68, imagined 0.72), because the failure set was dominated by one policy.

docs.title: Their number, my number
docs.text: Papers This arm False alarms at the registered α ≈ α by construction 22.7 % (α = 5 %) Failures caught logpZO top-1 in 10/16 settings; SAFE unseen AUROC 0.78 46 % Transfer across sessions "close to zero TNR" without new-setting successes (FAIL-Detect §VI) 42/42 successes flagged on the next session Policy-identity baseline not run 0.76, beats every probe

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
The unsupervised band fails on hardware the same way in Palo Alto and in Paris: the success distribution shifts with the setting and the band does not know. The supervised probe (SAFE's design) is the one that works on hardware in every paper I read, and the C1 result says my version of it is blocked on a confound the papers do not check — the failure labels came mostly from one policy. The register now requires a policy-identity and episode-length baseline under every monitor result, which neither paper runs.

Verdict: FAIL-Detect's band fails here as its authors warn it can; SAFE's probe is not yet tested cleanly.

What would change it: SAFE-MLP on SmolVLA's action-expert input features exported from vla.cpp, three random task splits, with episode length beside it.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 4: H-JEPA
docs.text: H-JEPA (Zhang, Terver, Rabbat, LeCun, Balestriero; arXiv 2610.06805) stacks LeWorldModels across timescales. I tested its level-2 slow feature as a progress signal (G6b) and it failed. Reading the paper afterwards, the paper's own Fig. 5 predicts that failure.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
Level 1 is LeWM. Each level ℓ > 1 has its own state encoder (a pointwise MLP over the level below), its own action encoder pooling s_ℓ lower actions, and its own causal predictor, stride 2 per level, all trained end-to-end with a LeWM loss per level. On real data (DROID) an inverse-dynamics term is required or the model collapses to "encode the predictable background, drop the arm" (their App. L). Planning is top-down by gradient descent: the top level plans macro-actions; its predicted states become subgoals for the level below.

Evaluation: four simulated environments; success rate; three paired model + planner seeds with SE; planner compute swept and reported as TFLOPs per episode; depth 1–4 at a fixed 100-TFLOP budget on 50 tasks per environment. Baseline HWM (same hierarchy, shared latent) separates "temporal decomposition" from "distinct abstract spaces". AntMaze 18 → 73 % at three levels; two levels match LeWM on Push-T, three levels fail there because episodes are short. The mechanism figure: probe NMSE per entity vs level shows body pose becoming unrecoverable while position stays; the entity-frequency gap (ratio of spectral centroids of fastest and slowest state components) predicts when this selective abstraction appears — above ~2× it does; Push-T, Cube and DROID have gaps below 2× and show none. On DROID the metric is Fréchet fidelity of the planned end-effector path against the expert's (15 clips, three seeds). No closed-loop real robot.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text: G6b. A level-2 slow feature (stride 15, SIGReg loss) on W1, tested as a progress signal on the bowls task. Bars: T1 Spearman between latent distance and time ≤ −0.80; false-stall rate ≤ 10 %; sanity AUROC ≥ 0.95. Result: T1 −0.73 (fail), false stalls 52 % (fail), sanity 0.998 (pass). The hierarchy was dropped.

I tested the hierarchy on data the paper says it should not change. There is no frequency gap on a single-arm pick-and-nest task; the paper's own prediction for that regime is "no selective abstraction", and that is what G6b found. So the negative result and the paper's claim do not conflict; the gate was outside the claim. What would change it: a task with a real timescale gap (a tidy loop with navigation-scale structure), which my bench does not have.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 1: LeWorldModel
docs.text:
One paper, one arm. This series takes each paper I actually tested on a SO-101 + Jetson Orin NX, states what the paper claims and how its authors measured it, puts my number next to theirs, and says what the gap means. Numbers are from journal/EXPERIMENTS.md; gate IDs are the register's.

LeWorldModel (Maes, Le Lidec, Scieur, LeCun, Balestriero; arXiv 2603.19312) is the recipe behind W1, the world model that runs on my arm. Four gates tested it: dynamics (G0), planning (G1b), progress (G6a), outcome readout (G10).

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
A 15M-parameter JEPA trained end-to-end from pixels: a ViT-tiny encoder (patch 14, 12 layers, width 192, ~5M) whose CLS token becomes one 192-d latent per frame; a 6-layer predictor with AdaLN zero-init action conditioning (~10M); loss ‖ẑ_{t+1} − z_{t+1}‖² + 0.1 · SIGReg, where SIGReg pushes the batch of latents toward an isotropic Gaussian by testing 1024 random 1-d projections for normality. No EMA target, no stop-gradient; SIGReg alone prevents collapse. Planning is CEM with a terminal cost ‖ẑ_H − z_g‖² inside MPC.

Evaluation is simulation only: Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, OGBench Cube. The headline is success at matched training FLOPs (Fig. 6): Push-T 90 % vs DINO-WM's 13 % at the same compute, planning 48× faster (0.98 s vs 47 s). Table 1 is a linear-probe table: a linear readout of the latent predicts Push-T block location with r = 0.986 and block angle with r = 0.902. There is no real robot, no non-learned planner baseline, and the authors list "short planning horizons" as the limitation.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
W1 is LeWM's recipe on 182 teleop episodes from two webcams (multi-view variant, ContactGuard-style mean-pool), 100 epochs, $3.30 on vast.ai.

G0, dynamics. Bar: beat copy-last; every action-corruption ratio ≥ 1.3 at K = 30; no collapse. Result: open-loop error at K = 30 0.31 vs copy-last 0.89; timing-shift ratios 1.99 / 1.58; effective rank 24–30 of 192 (the 5-epoch run was 5.8). Pass. The model learns real action-conditioned dynamics.

G1b, planning as ranking. Bar: rank the expert chunk first among 8 candidates at top-1 ≥ 0.8 at some horizon. Result: best 0.60 at d = 20–30. Fail. The diagnosis (G1 diagnosis row) found why: an action-only baseline with no model at all, ranking by commanded-joint distance, scores 0.68–0.90. On a position-controlled arm the commanded joints already determine the outcome of a 7-step chunk; the latent adds noise.

G6a, progress from latent distance. Bar: Spearman ≤ −0.8 between latent distance to goal and time. Result: −0.32 to −0.50. Fail. Latent distance is not progress here (the TD-JEPA paper, 2607.25337, finds the same gap in simulation: Spearman 0.65 for LeWM's Euclidean distance vs step count).

G10, outcome readout at rest. Bar: AUROC ≥ 0.90 on success/failure from the final latent. Result: 1.000. Pass. Table 1's probe result transfers: the latent contains the task outcome.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
Not that the paper is wrong. The paper's planner is compared to other learned planners at equal compute; it is never compared to "do nothing clever". On a cheap arm the clever-nothing baseline is strong because the commanded trajectory is the plan, and the latent planner has to beat it, not DINO-WM. The honest role for the model here is the one G10 passed: a verifier at rest. The planning-limits paper (2609.39235) later showed with a real simulator as a perfect predictor that terminal-latent-distance scoring against a distant goal falls from 92 % to 41 %; G1b scored against a goal many chunks away, so it sat in exactly that regime. A subgoal inside the rollout is the fix the paper proves; it has not been tried here yet.

Verdict: dynamics and readout reproduce; planning does not survive the baseline the paper did not run.

What would change it: G7 (object-state ranking where the joints are blind), with a near subgoal. That gate is frozen and waiting for a cube-rollout session.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 15: Real-Time Chunking
docs.text: Real-Time Chunking (Black, Galliker, Levine, Physical Intelligence; arXiv 2506.07339) treats the next action chunk as an inpainting problem. My gradient-free prefix overwrite is the paper's "hard mask" line, and the paper says where it should lose.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
With chunk length H, control period Δt and inference time δ, the delay is d = ⌊δ/Δt⌋ steps. Asynchronous inference must start the next chunk d steps early, and the junction is arbitrary: a new chunk from fresh noise may pick a different strategy (their bifurcation figure). Temporal ensembling averages across chunks and is not guaranteed valid when the distribution is multimodal. RTC: freeze the first d actions (they will be executed before the new chunk arrives), attend to the remaining overlap with an exponentially decaying weight, leave the rest free, and enforce it through ΠGDM guidance on the flow's velocity field with a clipped guidance weight — one vector-Jacobian product through the policy per Euler step. The soft mask (eq. 5): weight 1 for i < d, decaying over the overlap, 0 after.

Evaluation: twelve dynamic Kinetix tasks chosen because quasi-static benchmarks are saturated by open-loop chunking; 2 048 rollouts per point with Wilson 95 % intervals; delays 0–4; baselines naive async, BID, temporal ensembling. RTC is above every baseline at every delay; hard masking (freeze only d steps) is below soft masking at small d; temporal ensembling is worst even at d = 0. Real: π0.5, bimanual, H = 50, Δt = 20 ms, 5 denoising steps, d ≈ 6, plus +100 / +200 ms injected latency; six tasks, 10 trials per task per method per delay, metric throughput (task progress per minute). RTC is flat across added latency; synchronous falls linearly; both temporal-ensembling variants trip the protective stop at +100 ms and score zero. Cost: 97 vs 76 ms per chunk on their stack.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
G13b (2026-10-19, offline, Orin). SmolVLA on 20 bowls episodes, 254 chunk boundaries, d = 8 / 12 / 20. Methods: naive, exact RTC guidance, and gradient-free prefix overwrite. Bars: propose the gradient-free method if it cuts the median jump ≥ 50 % vs naive and stays within 20 % of exact. Result: prefix overwrite cuts the median jump 72–74 % at every d, drift unchanged; exact RTC cut only 21–41 % in this implementation (weaker than LeRobot's identity mode — flagged to check). Timing: naive 1 028 ms, overwrite 1 035 ms, exact 1 962 ms per chunk in PyTorch on the Orin; every method misses the 667 ms line because the policy itself is too slow in PyTorch.

In vla.cpp (same day). Ported as prev_actions + inference_delay; jump cut 71.0 / 73.3 / 71.5 % through the engine, prefix error 0.0, +0.4 ms per chunk, default path bit-identical. Exact RTC is not possible in vla.cpp today: ggml lacks backward rules for flash attention and concat.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
The overwrite is the paper's hard mask with the guidance weight sent to infinity on the frozen steps and zero elsewhere. The paper's Fig. 5 says that works and that soft masking beats it when d is small relative to H — which is my regime (d ≈ 7 of 50). That is a precise published prediction I have not tested, and testing it needs no engine work: implement eq. 5 in PyTorch, run the same 254 boundaries with shared noise, pair against the overwrite. Only if soft wins by more than the pairing noise are ggml backward kernels worth writing. And the result metric should be theirs: a smoother junction is for throughput; the jump is the instrument check, not the claim.

Verdict: the gradient-free point reproduces in spirit; the paper predicts a better point I have not measured.

What would change it: the soft-mask comparison offline, then throughput on the robot day with sync / async / async + prefix.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 8: ReAP
docs.text: ReAP (Liu, Qing, Wei, Hou; arXiv 2610.16309) trains a failure-supervised visual space and an action-conditioned risk predictor on top of it. My "ReAP-style risk head" is the closest any monitor got to my bar — and it is a stripped version with two confounds the paper's own design removes.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
Stage 1, a detector: frozen DINOv2 patches from each camera → Perceiver-style cross-attention from 32 learned queries → a compact state z_t → a risk head, trained with class-weighted BCE against a ramp target: 0 on successes, t/(T−1) on failures. No onset labels. Stage 2, a predictor: the policy's action chunk cross-attends the frozen latent, a residual MLP predicts the latent H steps ahead, and the frozen head reads risk from it; loss is latent-transition error plus risk BCE. Alarm = detector OR predictor, each with its own conformal threshold on held-out successes.

Metric bTWA: half earliness-weighted recall (a failure detected at t_i of T_i scores 1 − t_i/T_i) plus half specificity; averaged over five α; mean ± std over three seeds. Offline: LIBERO-10 and RoboTwin-8 with four policies; baselines from three families (action uncertainty, OOD, classifiers). ReAP 0.70–0.78 vs best baseline 0.58–0.76. Real: three π0.5 tasks, monitor live, alarms logged without acting. The ablations are the valuable part: a random, untrained detector scores 0.650 vs the learned 0.683 and mean-pooled DINOv2 beats every baseline alone (Table 3a); shuffled chunks from other episodes of the same task drop 0.683 → 0.618, zero actions → 0.52 (Table 3b). Detector latency 9.7 ms, no policy inference needed.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text: REAP monitors (2026-10-23). On W1-A's 50 episodes (42 ok / 8 fail), 5-fold × 5 seeds: W1 L2 surprise, a logistic or MLP risk head on [W1 latent, 30 commanded actions, step], elapsed time. Bar: ≥ 5/8 failures at ≤ 1/20 false interventions. Result: surprise 2/8 at 2/42 (AUROC 0.86); logistic head 6/8 at 7/42 (AUROC 0.93); MLP 7/8 at 13/42; elapsed 0/8. On all 69: logistic 23/25 at 4/44 (0.97), but 17 of the extra failures are TurboVLA's. Verdict: not proven. Two confounds: the secondary set's failures are mostly one policy, and the onsets were labelled by Gemini with two misses of 110 and 289 frames. Latency on the Orin: W1 tick 17.6 ms, 25-step imagination 153 ms off the control thread, risk head 18 ms; the policy's chunk slows 238 → 304 ms with the monitor sharing the GPU.
