docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
Table 3a says the encoder is not where my gap is: a random projection of DINOv2 is within 0.03 of their learned one, so W1's latent is probably fine. The two things their design has and mine lacks are exactly my two confounds. The ramp target removes the onset labels from the verdict — the 25 hand labels I owe become a validation set instead of a prerequisite. The shuffled-chunk control decides whether "action-conditioned" belongs in the name: train once, evaluate with other episodes' chunks; if the number does not drop, the head is a state monitor. Both are offline and free and are in the amendments; bTWA goes beside my bar so the comparison is on their metric too.

REAP v2 (2026-10-23, evening). The paper's own fixes applied: ramp target (no onset labels), no time feature, every episode cut to the task's common horizon (374 frames), shuffled-chunk and zero-action controls, bTWA reported, VLA-Corrector's parameter-free GRU as the floor. Protocol committed before the run. Result on the primary 50, medians over 5 seeds: logistic head 3/8 at 5/42, AUROC 0.789 (shuffled 0.708, zero 0.693); MLP 6/8 at 13/42; GRU floor 2/8 at 3/42, 0.589. So v1's 0.93 was the time feature and the episode length. The one thing that survives is the action-conditioning test: both W1 heads gain 0.07–0.08 over shuffled chunks, above the +0.05 line, so the head does read the commanded action — it just does not read enough.

Verdict: fail. No monitor meets the bar once the confounds are removed; the W1 risk head is action-conditioned but weak; the floor baseline is a state monitor.

What would change it: a world model trained on the deployed policy's own rollouts (ContactGuard's recipe), not teleop only; then the same v2 protocol.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 14: REKI
docs.text: REKI (Marrie, Pacaud, Ramanana Rahary, Chen, Böhle; Kyutai / Inria; arXiv 2610.22178) gives a VLA a memory through register tokens and measures the oscillation it removes. I voided my own latency measurement of it and then found the same oscillation in my policies with their metric.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
A 2.4B VLA (Qwen3.5-2B + a flow-matching expert) with 32 register tokens per frame in the expert: they cross-attend the frame's context, self-attend the registers of the K − 1 previous frames (K = 3), never read the action tokens, and are cached as keys/values across chunks — so memory costs +0.1 ms. Pretrained on public data only; 21.8 ms per chunk on an H100. The augmentation detail that matters for a webcam rig: random camera dropout and shuffled camera order, worth > 20 points under viewpoint change.

Evaluation: LIBERO-Plus 90.4; RoboTwin Clean2Rand 65.8; RoboCasa365 38.4; baselines quoted from their papers. The memory ablation (Fig. 5a): a K = 3 model evaluated at K = 1 scores like a K = 1 model — the gain comes from reading past frames at inference, mostly the first one. The oscillation result (Fig. 5b): an episode oscillates if an arm reverses direction at three or more consecutive chunks; 4.1 % with memory, 14.8 % when the same model is evaluated without it, 18.6 % trained without; two-arm tasks 24.5 → 3.1; RoboTwin, 50 tasks, 20 matched seeds each. Mechanism offered: perceptual aliasing — two poses each look like demonstration states heading toward the other.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
G12 (2026-10-18), voided the same day. The bar was memory ≤ 8 GB and chunk ≤ 250 ms on the Orin; the script reported 3.46 GB and 318 ms. The re-check found it timed a random-init Qwen2.5-1.5B with no vision tower and a hand-written random expert; the parts did not sum (135 + 230 ≠ 318). REKI's Orin latency is unmeasured.

G14 (2026-10-18). REKI's oscillation criterion on my 69 published rollouts: reversal at ≥ 3 consecutive chunks, cosine < −0.5, > 3° per chunk. Failed episodes 6/25 = 24.0 % (CI 11.5–43.4 %); succeeded 8/44; all episodes 14/69 = 20.3 %, which is the number comparable with REKI's (theirs is over all episodes). Trajectory check: the flagged failures are real re-grasp loops and pan dithering; two unflagged loops were missed. All my policies are memoryless.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
G14 is the cleanest external replication of a mechanism in my register: a memoryless policy on a SO-101 dithers at about the rate a memoryless 2.4B VLA dithers on RoboTwin, under the same definition. What I cannot yet say is whether memory fixes it here, because adding registers to SmolVLA means retraining. The paper's Fig. 5a points at the cheap half: for any policy that has a past-frame cache, the same checkpoint evaluated with and without it is a free experiment. SmolVLA has none, so the port is the only route, and it costs $5–10 plus a robot session; the amendments put the free comparison and the real latency measurement before it.

Verdict: the oscillation mechanism reproduces; the fix is untested; the latency gate was void and is to be redone.

What would change it: a real REKI chunk timed on the Orin with the released checkpoint, then 32 registers in SmolVLA's expert against the 20.3 % line.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 3: RoboJEPA
docs.text: RoboJEPA (Zholus, Assran et al., Meta FAIR; arXiv 2610.10515) is a scaling law for latent world models trained on 15 000 hours of robot video, including 21.5k LeRobot community episodes from arms like mine. Two gates: can the encoder run on the Orin, and does the pretrained predictor use my actions.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
A deterministic next-feature predictor on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1-G encoder (width 1664, patch 16). Per timestep the sequence is all views' patches plus an action token and a proprio token; attention is joint space-time-view, timestep-causal, local to 8 timesteps so it rolls out past its training length; QK-norm for stability. Loss is half teacher-forced L1, half autoregressive L1 from a prefix (the exposure-bias fix). 23 datasets, 12 embodiments, 26 action spaces; AdamW with a shared flat learning-rate stage and per-budget cool-downs.

The scaling law is of per-token L1 error over a 9-step latent rollout on held-out scenes (DROID holdout and RoboCasa), compute counted in FLOPs, compute-optimal frontier across 22M–2B. The functional form was chosen by extrapolation error on 4B and 8B held out of the fit (Table 2): a second-order law wins (0.6 / 1.4 ×10⁻³) over a plain power law (2.0 / 3.7). Downstream: closed-loop CEM planning in RoboCasa with capability emerging in order (end-effector control → holding → scene geometry → object dynamics, the last only at ~10²² FLOPs); a real Franka table (Table 3: 8B grasp 67 %, lift 50 %, pick-and-place 27 % success; π0.5 as a reference, not a baseline); "over 50 000 evaluation episodes" across both platforms, per-task n in an appendix. Planning is "several seconds per step for 8B, not real-time".

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
Gate B, encoder on device. Bar: 2-view encoder p50 ≤ 200 ms on the Orin NX. Result: 526 ms (one view 398 ms); the 100M predictor step 252 ms, 300M 487 ms. No-go on device. On the Mac (MPS) the encoder is 1 025 ms and the predictor's attention does not run. Any use is off-board on CUDA.

Gate A, does the pretrained predictor use my actions. Two bars on 9-step rollouts of my bowls latents: (1) L1 ≥ 15 % below copy-last for the 300M model; (2) ≥ 5 % below shuffled actions. Result: (1) 300M 11.8 %, 100M 10.5 %, 1B 15.8 % [14.6, 17.0] on only 30 clips; (2) 8.9–10.4 % for every size. The primary bar fails; the 1B is borderline on a partial sample; action conditioning works on my arm at every size.

G1b-RJ (the 1B on the ranking gate) was cancelled as a gate on 2026-10-15: neither outcome would change the build, since the encoder cannot run in the loop.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
My arm is in their training mix, and the pretrained model does read its actions — the Gate A shuffled-action margin is the far-left point of their scaling curve, at zero fine-tuning cost. What it cannot do is run where the arm is. The paper is explicit that planning is not real-time even on a GPU cluster; on an Orin the encoder alone eats sixteen control ticks. So the honest use is offline: feature extraction for a judge or a dataset-level probe. The method lesson is the one to keep: a scaling claim is an extrapolation test — fit on some sizes, predict the held-out ones, report the error. My own scaling angle (50 / 100 / 182 / 362 episodes) is a plot until it does that.

Verdict: action conditioning reproduces at the small end; the encoder is off the robot.

What would change it: a distilled encoder at ≤ 100 ms, which is not my experiment to run.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 10: Robometer
docs.text: Robometer (Liang, Korkmaz, Zhang, Hwang et al.; arXiv 2603.02115) is a 4B reward model trained on a million trajectories. I tested it zero-shot as a judge on my own rollouts and on a 2 099-rollout public SO-101 benchmark. Episode length beat it on every held-out task. The paper never computes episode length.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
Qwen3-VL-4B with learned tokens: a progress token after each frame (causal; progress in 10 bins, success at the last frame) and a preference token after two videos. Three losses: preference, progress, success. Pairs are built from expertise (expert vs failure), instruction negatives (same frames, wrong instruction → progress 0), and video rewind. Data: RBM-1M, 21 embodiments; SO-101 is not in it.

Evaluation on RBM-EVAL (976 OOD trajectories): VOC (Pearson r between predicted reward and frame index on successes) 0.92 and Kendall τ on the failed < suboptimal < successful ordering 0.64, vs RoboReward-8B 0.82 / 0.47. Zero-shot on RoboFAC, VOC 0.65. Ablations on LIBERO-90: adding failure data lifts τ from 0.74 to 0.92. Downstream: online RL on a DROID π0 base 20 → 85 % (20 trials); offline IQL on SO-101 "2.4× the best baseline" (0.85 vs 0.50 on an oven task; 0.15 vs 0.05 on a plate task — 3 vs 1 successes in 20); failure detection on 100 DROID trajectories, F1 0.81 vs GPT-5-mini 0.33. The authors' own limitation: no access to contact or grasp stability.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
G9a-AB (2026-10-15/16). Zero-shot on ArmnetBench, 2 099 rollouts, 7 policies, top camera. Bar: pooled AUROC ≥ 0.85 and within-policy ≥ 0.8 on ≥ 5/7. Complete set: pooled 0.818 [0.790, 0.843]; within-policy 5/7; episode length alone 0.938; beyond length (quintile median 0.687, CV gain +0.016) both bars missed. Fail: not a zero-shot judge.

G9a-own (2026-10-16). On my 88 labelled bowls rollouts: AUROC 0.577 [0.44, 0.70]; TPR 0.25 at the calibrated threshold; policy identity 0.878; wrong-object failures scored highest. Fail.

G9b (written 2026-10-22). The LoRA fine-tune on held-out-task folds never trained (the job died at preprocessing). The zero-shot baseline on policy rollouts only: stack 0.564, tool 0.616, cable 0.761, ring 0.933; length 0.903 / 0.855 / 0.946 / 0.965, better on 4/4; CV gain over length +0.008 [−0.001, 0.017]. No verdict.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
Robometer and my result agree once the question is phrased right. The model answers "how far along does this look" and does that well (VOC 0.92 is real). My failure mode is identity — the wrong bowl, nested — and a trajectory-comparison objective with instruction negatives at the dataset level has no reason to catch it at the frame level on an embodiment it never saw. The paper's own "pull tissue" and "fold towel" rows (F1 0.58, 0.76) are its version of the same gap. The number that should be in every reward-model paper and is in none of the ten I read: episode length. On my tasks it is the judge every learned judge must beat first.

Verdict: fails as a zero-shot judge on this arm; the gap is the task's, not the model's.

What would change it: an instruction-negative test on my own frames (swap the instruction, fix the frames, does the score move?) before any LoRA; and labels for suboptimal-but-successful episodes, which τ needs and I do not have.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 11: SmolVLA
docs.text: SmolVLA (Shukor, Aubakirova, Capuano et al., Hugging Face; arXiv 2506.01844) is the policy behind almost every number on this site. Its paper's ablation tables are the manual for running it on a Jetson; three of them predicted things I later measured.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
A 450M VLA: SmolVLM-2 (SigLIP + SmolLM2) with the image at 512×512, no tiling, pixel-shuffled to 64 visual tokens per frame; the state projected to one token into the VLM prefix; only the first 16 of 32 LLM layers run; a ~100M action expert alternating cross-attention (to the VLM's keys/values) and causal self-attention over the chunk, trained by conditional flow matching with 10 Euler steps, chunk 50. Only the expert is trained. Pretraining: 481 community SO-100 datasets, 22.9k episodes, with task strings rewritten by a VLM and cameras manually mapped to a consistent order.

Evaluation: LIBERO and Meta-World at 10 trials per task; real SO-100 and SO-101 tasks with 50 demos each (10 per 5 start positions), scored by sub-steps; baselines π0 fine-tuned on the same data and ACT from scratch. Headline: LIBERO 87.3 for 0.45B vs π0 86.0; SO-100 real 78.3 vs π0 61.7 vs ACT 48.3; SO-101 LEGO 90 / 50 in-/out-of-distribution. The ablations: community pretraining is worth +27 points on SO-100 (Table 5); cross+self attention 85.5 vs cross-only 79.0; flow matching 80.3 vs L1 75.3; state in the VLM prefix 80.3 vs in the expert 73.3 (Table 11); chunk 50 fine; and executing 1 / 10 / 30 / 50 actions before re-observing: 80.3 / 82.8 / 70.8 / 51.8 (Table 13). Asynchronous inference keeps success (73.3 vs 78.3) and doubles throughput (19 vs 9 cubes in fixed time). No seeds, no intervals.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
The bowls gate (10 trials, operator-judged). SmolVLA PyTorch on the Orin: 9/10 at 974 ms per chunk. Through vla.cpp: 9/10 at 390 ms; with flash attention 8/10 at 238 ms. Same weights, 4× faster, same task success. The task is at ceiling (ACT 9–10/10, VLA-JEPA 9/10), so it separates engines, not policies.

Parity. The GGUF against PyTorch on fixed frames and shared noise: median max |Δ| 0.80° against a 1° line (noise-to-noise spread in PyTorch itself 12.2°).

Chunk boundaries (G13b, G13b-in-vla.cpp). With a 238 ms chunk at 30 Hz the inference delay is d ≈ 7 steps; a fresh chunk from fresh noise jumps at the junction. Gradient-free prefix overwrite cuts the median jump 72–74 % offline and 71–73 % through the engine at +0.4 ms per chunk.

Oscillation (G14). 24 % of failed episodes reverse direction at ≥ 3 consecutive chunks.

docs.text:
Nothing here contradicts the paper; the paper predicts the work. Table 13 is my boundary problem in the authors' own numbers: executing a whole chunk before re-observing is ruinous, re-observing every ≤ 10 steps is nearly free — if the junction is handled, which is what prefix overwrite and RTC are for. Table 11 is a checklist item for the plugin (state in the prefix, not the expert). Table 5 is the honest footnote under every fine-tune: the community pretraining is doing more than any architecture choice I could make. The one thing I measured that the paper does not is the engine: on an Orin the first 4× is engineering, and the control-loop research cannot start until it is done.

Verdict: reproduces; the ablation tables are the operating manual.

What would change it: nothing needs changing; the open question from this paper on my arm is the async stack's refill threshold g, which I run through vla.cpp and have not pre-registered.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 12: TurboVLA
docs.text: TurboVLA (Xie, Yao, Wu et al.; arXiv 2607.27205) drops the language model from the VLA and binds vision to text with Grounding-DINO-style cross-attention. My port failed on a two-task dataset, I concluded it ignored the instruction, then I found my port differed from the paper in four places, then I ran the paper's own trainer on my data. The faithful model ignores the instruction too. The data was the whole story.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
V + L → A instead of V → L → A: DINOv3 patch features and BERT token features, each projected to 256-d, fused by six bidirectional cross-attention layers initialised from Grounding DINO (--pretrained_init_ckpt groundingdino_swint_ogc.pth), then an ACT-style decoder with 12 learnable action queries; the robot state enters the decoder memory only (eq. 6/9), because "it is required for translating task-conditioned scene features into executable actions but not necessary for visual-language correspondence". Plain ℓ1 on the chunk. 0.2B parameters, 31 ms per chunk on a 4090.

Evaluation: LIBERO with one mixed-suite model, 50 rollouts per task, 97.7 average (π0.5 96.9 at 3× the latency, SmolVLA 88.8); RoboTwin 2.0 multi-task 60.2; real Piper, four tasks, 40 trials each, against π0.5 on the same data. The ablation that matters here, Table 3: remove language, LIBERO average 97.7 → 70.8, LIBERO-Goal 97.4 → 11.6. On data where the instruction is the only thing that distinguishes targets, this architecture uses it. One-way cross-attention costs 1.2–1.6 points (Table 5). The Grounding DINO initialisation is stated once and never ablated.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
Several variants, Sept 29 – Oct 8. 0/3 on the last; a two-week diagnosis with six probes concluded the model ignored the instruction on the two-task bowls data. The data finding survived: on 94 % of frames the instruction is redundant with the arm state ("fact 7": the side decision is visible in ~6 % of frames and the pose leaks it), so a copycat policy fits the data.

The port review (2026-10-22). Against upstream turbovla/models/: (1) the six fusion layers were random-init in every variant — the checkpoint converter transferred DINOv3 only; (2) the fusion block is a different module — two independent cross-attentions instead of BiAttentionBlock (shared affinity, layer-scale 1e-4, drop-path) plus a text self-attention layer; (3) the state token was prepended to vision before fusion instead of entering the decoder memory; (4) decoder depth, head and normalisation differ. So "TurboVLA ignores the instruction" was never established; a port that ignores it was.

Faithful reproduction, step 1 (2026-10-22). The free control: upstream code, released LIBERO checkpoint, task swap over the ten LIBERO-Goal instructions on 40 frames. Threshold 0.095 normalised (= 5° of SO-101 pan). Result 0.105 — the real model moves its actions when the instruction changes; my port moved 0.1–0.25°, 20–55× less. Path A was frozen on that number: task swap ≥ 5° with per-layout ≥ 75 % → the port was the bug; task swap < 1° with the control ≥ 0.095 → fact 7.

Faithful reproduction, path A (2026-10-23). Upstream's own trainer on the bowls data, full LIBERO init (666 of 672 tensors transferred; the 6 width-dependent ones re-initialised), 35k steps, batch 64 (128 OOM on 24 GB), ≈ $2.0 plus ~$0.8 of failed starts. Result: task swap 0.020° (frames 0.006–0.053°), per-layout 38.9 %, start reach 26.7°; the control still 0.105. The paper's recipe, with the paper's initialisation and the paper's fusion block, moves its actions by two hundredths of a degree when the instruction changes on this data. Fact 7 is the full story.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
Two claims, now both answered. The data claim stands and is now the whole result: on frames where the instruction is redundant with the arm state 94 % of the time, the paper's architecture with the paper's weights learns the copycat too (0.020° vs 0.105 for the same model on LIBERO-Goal, where the instruction is decisive). The model claim — that my port was the reason — is false: the four divergences are real, documented, and made no difference to instruction use. Table 3 of the paper and path A together say the same thing from two sides: this architecture reads language exactly when the data makes language necessary, and not otherwise. A by-product: the Grounding DINO initialisation, never ablated in the paper, is ablated here on one dataset (random vs faithful) with no effect on the quantity that mattered.

The lesson I am keeping is about order, not architecture: parity against upstream should have come before the two-week diagnosis, and the diagnosis should have ended with a data-side control (train the paper's model on data where the instruction is decisive) before any sentence about the model. Both are now rules in the register.

Verdict: the data claim (fact 7) is the full story; the port claim is withdrawn; correction row written.

What would change it: nothing about this dataset. The next test is the paper's model on data where the instruction decides early and often (the tidy-loop sessions), which is the only way to learn whether it helps on this arm.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 9: VLA-Corrector
docs.text: VLA-Corrector (Song, Qian, Feng, Song; arXiv 2609.06508) wraps a frozen π0.5 in a tiny learned verifier that routes a recovery prompt. I borrowed one of its signals — cosine drift of the latent — as a monitor. It caught nothing. The part of the paper I should have borrowed is the verifier's design.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
The policy is frozen (OpenPI pi05_libero). The verifier reads only observable history: two 112×112 views → parameter-free spatial statistics (3×4×4 pooled RGB plus mean and std, 54 features per view) → Linear 64; state and action → MLP 32; a GRU over an 8-step window; two heads, binary risk and a five-way stage. Teacher labels come from a rule-based state machine on simulator state (f = 1 within 10 steps of a failure event, 0 beyond 20). Gate: τ = 0.40, four consecutive positive windows, 10-step cooldown; the stage selects a recovery prompt fragment appended to the instruction; up to 100 recovery actions, then the original instruction resumes. Verifier training: 120 episodes, 30 epochs, CPU; 0.46 ms inference.

Evaluation: LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus difficulty 4–5 under action noise, target shift, goal shift and all three, 1 000 episodes per condition; three configurations — no assistance, a privileged rule verifier (the efficacy upper bound), the learned verifier. Combined perturbation 70.7 → 82.6 (rule) / 80.2 (learned): the learned verifier is within 2.4 points of the oracle. Verifier quality: accuracy 93.1 %, precision 61.1 %, recall 94.9 %, AUROC 0.90; recovery success 75 %. Ablations: single frame −15 F1, state-action only −15.8. Real arm (unnamed), three tasks, 40 trials each, target moved after execution starts: 82.5 → 88.3 average, zero-shot from sim-trained features.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
W1-A (2026-10-19). Cosine drift of W1's latent as a mid-rollout screener on 50 episodes, beside L2 surprise and the live reflex. Bar: ≥ 5/8 failures at ≤ 1/20 false interventions. Result: cosine drift 0/8, AUROC 0.30 — below chance; L2 surprise 2/8 at 2/42; the live reflex flagged 42/42 successes. Fail.

I never built the paper's verifier itself.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
Cosine drift was a wrong borrowing — the paper's verifier is not a drift threshold. Two things from the paper matter more than the result. First, the precision/recall split: a 61 % / 95 % verifier is a usable gate when a false trigger costs a re-prompt rather than a trial. My monitor bar (≤ 1/20 false interventions) assumes the expensive kind; if the intervention is "re-observe and re-prompt", the bar can relax and the 6/8-at-7/42 risk head from the ReAP post may already be a useful gate. Second, the parameter-free front end plus a GRU reaches 0.90 on LIBERO at zero cost on the Orin; it is the right floor baseline to put under any W1-based monitor, and it is now in the amendments as one.

Verdict: the borrowed signal fails; the paper's verifier is untested here and is the next floor baseline.

What would change it: the 54-feature GRU on my 69 rollouts, beside the risk head, with the recovery cost stated in the bar.

docs.title: Paper vs hardware 13: VLA-JEPA
docs.text: VLA-JEPA (Sun, Zhang, Qi et al.; arXiv 2602.10098) pretrains a VLA on human video through a latent world model. I trained it for $10, ran it on the arm at 9/10, and tested whether its eight samples were worth choosing between. The paper's honest ablation row says what to expect: robustness, not accuracy.

docs.title: What the paper claims, and how it measures it
docs.text:
A Qwen3-VL backbone with a flow-matching head. Latent-action tokens are read out of the VLM given the initial frame only plus the instruction — no future frame ever enters the VLM, which is the leakage-free principle — and an autoregressive latent world model predicts frozen V-JEPA 2 state chunks from them; L_WM is the teacher-forced prediction error. Robot data adds action tokens after the latent ones and a flow-matching loss; the joint objective is L_FM + β L_WM. Pretrained on Something-Something-v2 (220k human videos) and DROID; fine-tuned per benchmark.

Evaluation: LIBERO at 500 episodes per suite, 97.2 vs π0.5 96.9 — and 96.1 without human video (+1.1). SimplerEnv: Google Robot 65.2 with human video, 78.4 without (the authors attribute the reversal to the real-to-sim gap). LIBERO-Plus, seven perturbation axes: 79.5 vs OpenVLA-OFT 69.6, and 62.9 without human video (+16.6, the number the paper is about). Real Franka, 100 demos, three tasks: 0.70 vs π0 0.57 in distribution. No intervals; ±1 on LIBERO is inside binomial noise at this n.

docs.title: What I ran
docs.text:
Training. Qwen3-VL-2B + DiT-B, world model off at inference, ~$9.7 on vast.ai over two days.

The bowls gate. 9/10 on the Orin NX at 355 ms per chunk (PyTorch); in the twelve-VLA latency benchmark through vla.cpp, 177 ms minimum.

H0 (2026-10-08). The question the policy's design invites: do its 8 flow samples vary enough that picking one with a world model would help? Bars: oracle/mean error ≤ 0.7, latency at N = 8 ≤ 1.5×, baseline success < 85 %. Result: 0.76 (null 0.92); 1.84× (643 vs 349 ms); baseline 90 %. No-go. Averaging the eight chunks got 45 % of the oracle's gain with no model at all. Reranking was dropped the same day, and with it the first architecture version.

docs.title: What the gap means
docs.text:
The paper's own ablation rows say the human-video pretraining buys robustness to perturbation, not nominal accuracy, and sometimes costs accuracy (SimplerEnv). A nominal gate at ceiling, which is all I ran, cannot see that and did not. If I ever run a perturbation gate — lighting, background, camera — this paper predicts which policy survives and why; a nominal gate showing no difference would confirm it, not refute it. The H0 result is mine, not theirs: the samples do not differ enough to be worth a chooser, and the cheapest chooser (the mean) is half as good as an oracle for free. That one afternoon ended a design.

Verdict: trains and runs as advertised; the robustness claim is untested here; sample reranking is a no-go.

What would change it: a perturbation gate against SmolVLA on the same layouts, after the camera question (SEVO) is settled.
